The manifest goes brief — killing the 95.7 KB session-start tax

Every agent session opens with bp capabilities -o json: 95,666 bytes of full-depth manifest landing where the meter amplifies bytes 5-6x. It is the last un-briefed first-party payload and the spend census's top-ranked prize. This wave makes the agent-facing manifest born brief — 17.5-24.3 KB, invoke-complete, deterministic — verified by count_tokens on the ready fixtures and one live before/after session. Riding along: the two seals the user ratified as NOW (query.ex's unsealed task-embed chain, the nil-polarity inversion), because the doctrine orders seal before tiers and this is the first tier wave of the epic.

Wave 1 of the ctx-compression epic · epic task task-495cc9a9af43472c · charter: .claude/workflows/bp-ctx-compression-charter.md (founded at Decide, pushed 4b46ccbe6) · ground truth: /papers/ctx-compression-capstone + five lane papers · all 12 capstone judgment calls RATIFIED 2026-07-24
The wish (verbatim)

Alright, 1 then 2 — user's verbatim approval of: ratify the context-compression epic (task-495cc9a9af43472c) and charter it via bp-epic-cycle with wave 1 first. Wave 1 is the capstone's top-ranked win: the manifest brief view — the last un-briefed first-party payload, 95,666 B → 17.5-24.3 KB (3.9-5.5x), paid on every session; verification = count_tokens on the fixtures + one live before/after session. All 12 capstone judgment calls are RATIFIED on the recommended column (recorded in the epic task's notes): audit-wrap duel RUNS inside the cage spec pre-registered; brief-v3 squeak accepted; board profile ruling stands; bp park = plugin + 2 MB ceiling + mandatory summary; nil-polarity flip + fence; seal query.ex NOW; axi-b7 write echoes ?view=brief opt-in; ?views=1 stays opt-in; schema evolution on rev-pinned reads FAILS CLOSED; census thresholds forbidden until measured; duel budget ~$30-80; board clamp raise-then-fold (the raise already landed as stopgap PR #6033 / task-8ad8d5cfe98c70aa — coordinate, don't duplicate it). Ground truth papers: /papers/ctx-compression-capstone (crown), -headroom-lessons, -spend-census, -handle-doctrine, -view-tiers-seam, -taskboard-flagship. Doctrine: compress presentation, never truth; native-only; count_tokens before token claims; seal before tiers.
Direction — born-brief session start, rendered where the truth already lives

The finished experience: an agent opens a session, runs bp capabilities -o json (or gets it piped), and receives a brief manifest — roughly 17.5-24.3 KB instead of 95.7 KB — that is INVOKE-COMPLETE: every noun, every verb, every arg (name/required/type), every flag (name/type), every summary an agent needs to compose ANY bp command correctly on the first try, with zero follow-up calls. What vanishes is exactly the plumbing only the CLI itself consumes: http method/path templates, mutation_op, set_key, scoped_prefix, default_output, dry_run/batch bookkeeping. bp capabilities --full remains byte-identical to today's output — the escape hatch is one flag, named in the brief itself. Humans see no change: the -o table tree was already brief.

The load-bearing structural insight from reading the real code: the wire is NOT where this payload is paid. internal/manifest/fetch.go always fetches (and ETag-caches) the FULL manifest because the CLI's entire command tree is a pure function of it — that fetch never enters agent context. The 95,666 B enters context as STDOUT: runCapabilities (internal/cli/builtins.go:44) re-marshals the strict-decoded Manifest struct and prints it. So the diet belongs at the point of print: a deterministic brief projection in Go, over truth the client provably holds in full. This is not a proxy guessing — it is the system's own first-party CLI projecting its own strict-decoded contract, which is exactly what 'compress presentation, never truth' permits.

Tentative key choices (Decide finalizes after two explore rounds): (1) render client-side in runCapabilities under exactly the AXI option-B semantics — brief when machineOut() AND NOT --full; explicit -o table unchanged; (2) the brief SHAPE is decided by measurement, not taste: caps_brief.json (24,266 B) vs caps_brief.tsv (17,543 B) go through count_tokens — bytes are not tokens and the meter standard bans tiktoken/chars-4 — with the pre-committed rule that tokens win, ties break toward JSON (parseability); (3) the projection spec ships as a named keep-list artifact so a later server-side ?view=brief (for SDK/curl consumers, if a future census ever ranks them) adopts it verbatim — nothing foreclosed; (4) the slice carries the full AXI protective-pattern kit in the same PR: byte tripwire pair (realistic + hostile), exact-key-set pin, opt-out-byte-identical proof for --full, determinism check (byte-identical consecutive calls — already true today, must stay true); (5) invoke-completeness is an acceptance TEST, not a hope: for every command in the manifest, the brief alone must carry what composing that command requires.

Companion slices, small and ratified NOW: (a) seal Tasks.Query.to_render_map (query.ex:740-753) by copying board.ex's field_readable? gate verbatim, with the redact-then-assert-omitted proof — the doctrine orders seal before tiers, and this is tier wave one; (b) flip the nil-polarity inversion (envelope.ex:222 field_readable? nil => true) and fence it so the next hand-rolled emitter cannot pass nil believing it fails closed. Candidate micro-slice if survey confirms it is as cheap as the census claims: a did-you-mean hint for bp task show / bp task list — 2,428 + 329 typed occurrences, 1.19 MB of pure error waste with no defenders. Verification for the flagship: 12 count_tokens calls on the fixtures (epic task #1 per the capstone) plus one live before/after agent session on the ledger measuring total_cost_usd, num_turns, and --full escape-hatch rate.
Brief-but-complete beats smaller-but-lossy: a card missing one needed field costs more than the cut saved.

Explicitly OUT of this wave: the board tier and rev-everywhere (later waves per the ratified order), the serialization duel proper (wave 2, duel-gated, $30-80 budget), bp park and MCP (wave 3+, after exercise), the ETag-view cache-key fold and Vary emission (needed only when a server-side view ships — this direction avoids triggering that RFC 9110 fix now), and anything touching taskboard fetch (stopgap PR #6033 / task-8ad8d5cfe98c70aa is in flight there — coordinate, don't duplicate).
Direction debate — three candidates, one winner

Candidate A — server-side ?view=brief on GET /v1/capabilities, under the views grammar. The doctrine-pure reading ('the brief card is a server render'): Elixir hand-tunes a brief manifest, every consumer (CLI, MCP, SDK, curl) inherits it, the tier grammar stays uniform. It loses on engineering economics that only appear once you read the consumption path: the CLI must fetch the FULL manifest regardless (the command tree is built from it), so a server brief saves zero wire and zero context on its own — it only changes what gets PRINTED, which a client projection does identically. And it drags in real scope: the ETag must fold the view param (the capstone flags today's precedent as a latent RFC 9110 violation that MUST be fixed by whoever ships a server view), Vary must be emitted, a second wire shape needs Go strict-decode modeling plus the frozen manifest.schema.json additive dance, across two languages. All of that to produce byte-identical stdout. The views grammar also structurally cannot describe the capabilities builtin — it is the bootstrap (chicken-and-egg: you need the manifest to learn what views exist), a carve-out today and a carve-out under A.

Candidate B (WINNER) — client-side deterministic brief projection at the point of print. One language, zero wire-contract risk (released binaries strict-decode the manifest; stdout shape is not a wire contract and carries no DisallowUnknownFields blast radius), works offline against the on-disk ETag cache, and the render is a pure function of strict-decoded truth — when the server adds a command tomorrow, the brief includes it with zero code change, preserving the manifest package's 'hardcodes NO noun' law. The count_tokens-validated keep-list is the durable artifact; it ports verbatim to a server view the day a measured non-CLI consumer exists.

Candidate C — shrink the manifest itself (trim summaries/flag docs for everyone). Rejected fastest: the summaries ARE the product for the human tree and the MCP tool derivation, the root shape is frozen under strict decode, and it compresses truth to fix a presentation problem — a direct doctrine violation.

Sharpest attacks on the winner, and how the wave absorbs them: (1) DOCTRINE DRIFT — every other brief is server-declared; this forks the grammar. Absorbed: capabilities is already outside the grammar (a builtin the views descriptor cannot reach), the projection is first-party and guess-free, and the keep-list is written to be server-portable — the fork is a deferral, not a divergence. (2) COMPLETENESS RISK — the census's own law says a brief missing one field costs more than it saves (agents already handle-climb 12,368 task gets vs 1,421 readies). Absorbed: invoke-completeness is the acceptance test, and the live before/after session measures the --full escape rate directly; if agents climb, the brief fattens before it ships. (3) BYTES ARE NOT TOKENS — TSV wins bytes (17.5 vs 24.3 KB) but JSON punctuation vs TSV structure may invert on the tokenizer, and 'count_tokens before token claims' is ratified doctrine. Absorbed: the shape choice is explicitly deferred to the count_tokens run — task #1 of the wave, pre-committed decision rule. (4) HIDDEN CONSUMERS — a script somewhere parses bp capabilities -o json and breaks on brief-when-piped. Absorbed: survey question manifest-consumers censuses every parser in the repo before Decide; the AXI piped-default precedent survived the same worry with option-B semantics.

Direction debate — three candidates, one winner

Candidate A — server-side ?view=brief on GET /v1/capabilities, under the views grammar. The doctrine-pure reading ('the brief card is a server render'): Elixir hand-tunes a brief manifest, every consumer (CLI, MCP, SDK, curl) inherits it, the tier grammar stays uniform. It loses on engineering economics that only appear once you read the consumption path: the CLI must fetch the FULL manifest regardless (the command tree is built from it), so a server brief saves zero wire and zero context on its own — it only changes what gets PRINTED, which a client projection does identically. And it drags in real scope: the ETag must fold the view param (the capstone flags today's precedent as a latent RFC 9110 violation that MUST be fixed by whoever ships a server view), Vary must be emitted, a second wire shape needs Go strict-decode modeling plus the frozen manifest.schema.json additive dance, across two languages. All of that to produce byte-identical stdout. The views grammar also structurally cannot describe the capabilities builtin — it is the bootstrap (chicken-and-egg: you need the manifest to learn what views exist), a carve-out today and a carve-out under A.

Candidate B (WINNER) — client-side deterministic brief projection at the point of print. One language, zero wire-contract risk (released binaries strict-decode the manifest; stdout shape is not a wire contract and carries no DisallowUnknownFields blast radius), works offline against the on-disk ETag cache, and the render is a pure function of strict-decoded truth — when the server adds a command tomorrow, the brief includes it with zero code change, preserving the manifest package's 'hardcodes NO noun' law. The count_tokens-validated keep-list is the durable artifact; it ports verbatim to a server view the day a measured non-CLI consumer exists.

Candidate C — shrink the manifest itself (trim summaries/flag docs for everyone). Rejected fastest: the summaries ARE the product for the human tree and the MCP tool derivation, the root shape is frozen under strict decode, and it compresses truth to fix a presentation problem — a direct doctrine violation.

Absorbed: capabilities is already outside the grammar (a builtin the views descriptor cannot reach), the projection is first-party and guess-free, and the keep-list is written to be server-portable — the fork is a deferral, not a divergence. Absorbed: the shape choice is explicitly deferred to the count_tokens run — task #1 of the wave, pre-committed decision rule.
